title: Keyboard Shortcuts
summary: One consolidated bank of Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, browser and function-key shortcuts. The syllabus names keyboard shortcuts explicitly, and 2-4 of the 20 CKT questions are pure shortcut recall, so these are the cheapest marks in the module.

subtopics.title: Windows 10/11 and File Explorer shortcuts
subtopics.concept:
The **Windows key (Win)** shortcuts control the desktop itself. Most are the same in Windows 10 and Windows 11.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Win | Open/close Start menu |
| Win+D | Show desktop (press again to restore windows) |
| Win+M / Win+Shift+M | Minimise all windows / restore them |
| Win+E | Open File Explorer |
| Win+L | Lock the PC |
| Win+R | Run dialog (type cmd, calc, notepad...) |
| Win+I | Settings |
| Win+S | Search |
| Win+X | Quick Link (power user) menu |
| Win+V | Clipboard history (multiple copied items) |
| Win+Shift+S | Snip part of the screen (Snipping Tool) |
| Win+PrtScn | Save a full-screen screenshot to Pictures\Screenshots |
| Alt+PrtScn | Copy only the active window to the clipboard |
| Win+. (or Win+;) | Emoji panel |
| Win+Tab | Task View (all open windows + desktops) |
| Win+Ctrl+D / Win+Ctrl+F4 | New virtual desktop / close current one |
| Win+Ctrl+Left/Right | Switch virtual desktops |
| Win+Left/Right/Up/Down | Snap left/right, maximise, minimise/restore |
| Win+Z | Snap layouts (Windows 11) |
| Win+P | Project/display mode (second screen) |
| Alt+Tab | Switch between open windows |
| Alt+F4 | Close the active window (on the desktop: Shut Down dialog) |
| Ctrl+Shift+Esc | Open Task Manager directly |
| Ctrl+Alt+Del | Security screen (lock, sign out, Task Manager) |

**File Explorer:** F2 rename; F3 search box; F5 refresh; Ctrl+Shift+N new folder; Alt+Enter Properties; Alt+Up go up one folder; Alt+Left back; Delete moves to Recycle Bin, **Shift+Delete deletes permanently**; Ctrl+A select all; Ctrl+click selects scattered files; Shift+click selects a range.

tricks.title: Win + first letter
tricks.body: Most Win shortcuts use the first letter of the action: **E**xplorer, **L**ock, **R**un, **I** (settIngs), **S**earch, **D**esktop, **M**inimise, **P**roject, **V** (paste history, like Ctrl+V). Learn the letter and you know the key.

example.q: Win+R opens?
example.solution: The Run dialog (R = Run).

tricks.title: Alt = Active window
tricks.body: Alt shortcuts act on the window in front of you: Alt+Tab switches it, Alt+F4 closes it, Alt+PrtScn captures only it, Alt+Enter shows the selected item's properties.

example.q: Which key captures only the active window?
example.solution: Alt+PrtScn.

mistakes: Mixing up Ctrl+Shift+Esc (Task Manager directly) and Ctrl+Alt+Del (security screen with a Task Manager option).
Thinking Win+M toggles like Win+D - Win+M only minimises; Win+Shift+M or Win+D brings windows back.
Saying Delete removes a file permanently - it goes to the Recycle Bin; only Shift+Delete skips it.
subtopics.notes:
### The Windows key family
The **Win key** (the flag between Ctrl and Alt) controls the desktop itself. Most shortcuts use the **first letter of the action** — E for Explorer, L for Lock, R for Run:

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Win | Open or close the Start menu |
| **Win+D** | Show the desktop; press again to restore windows |
| **Win+E** | Open File Explorer |
| **Win+L** | **Lock** the computer |
| **Win+R** | Open the **Run** dialog (type cmd, calc, notepad) |
| **Win+I** | Open Settings |
| **Win+S** | Search |
| Win+M / Win+Shift+M | Minimise all windows / restore them |
| Win+Tab | Task view (all virtual desktops and windows) |
| Win+Left/Right/Up/Down | Snap the window to half or quarter of the screen |
| Win+PrtScn | Screenshot saved to Pictures |
| Win+Shift+S | Snip a selected part of the screen |
| Win+V | Clipboard history (several copied items) |

Traps: **Win+M only minimises** (no toggle); Win+D toggles. Win+E is files; a browser is not Explorer.

### The security trio
| Combo | What appears |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Shift+Esc** | **Task Manager directly** — fastest route |
| **Ctrl+Alt+Del** | The full-screen security menu (Lock, Switch user, Task Manager…) |
| Alt+F4 | Close the active program (on the desktop it opens the shutdown dialog) |

### File Explorer moves
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Shift+N** | New folder |
| **F2** | Rename the selected item |
| **Alt+Enter** | Properties of the selected item |
| **Alt+Up arrow** | Go up one folder level |
| **Delete** | To Recycle Bin; **Shift+Delete** = permanent |
| Ctrl+A | Select everything |

### Switching and closing
- **Alt+Tab** — switch between open windows (hold Alt, tap Tab).
- **Win+D** or Win+M — clear the screen to the desktop.
- **Win+arrows** — park a window on half the screen (snapping), great for comparing two documents.

### How exam questions sound
| The stem says | Answer |
|---|---|
| "opens File Explorer" | Win+E |
| "locks the computer" | Win+L |
| "opens the Run dialog" | Win+R |
| "Task Manager directly" | Ctrl+Shift+Esc |
| "switches between open programs" | Alt+Tab |
| "closes the active program" | Alt+F4 |
| "creates a new folder" | Ctrl+Shift+N |
| "renames the selected file" | F2 |

Ten-second method: read the **verb** (switch / close / open / lock), pick the **family** (Win-key, Alt, Ctrl+Shift), then apply the first-letter rule and eliminate the planted nonsense option.

### Quick revision
- First-letter rule: E = Explorer, L = Lock, R = Run, I = settings (I for 'yes, change it').
- Win+D toggles the desktop; Win+M only minimises (Win+Shift+M restores).
- Task Manager direct = Ctrl+Shift+Esc; the security screen = Ctrl+Alt+Del.
- Explorer: Ctrl+Shift+N new folder, F2 rename, Alt+Enter properties, Alt+Up up one level.
- Alt+Tab switches windows; Alt+F4 closes the program.

patterns.name: Win-key shortcut recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which shortcut opens File Explorer / locks the PC / opens the Run dialog?' — a Win-key action with four combos as options.
patterns.logic:
1. First-letter rule: Win+E Explorer, Win+L Lock, Win+R Run, Win+I settings.
2. Distinguish near pairs: Win+D toggles the desktop, Win+M only minimises; Win+V clipboard history, Win+Shift+S snip.
3. Eliminate combos whose letter contradicts the action (Win+P for Lock is planted nonsense — P is projection).

example.q: Which shortcut **locks** the computer so a password is needed to return?
example.solution: **Win+L** — L for Lock. Win+D shows the desktop; Alt+F4 closes programs.

patterns.name: Task Manager and security combos
patterns.howToSpot: 'Direct shortcut for Task Manager', 'what does Ctrl+Alt+Del show?', 'which combo ends a not-responding program fastest?'
patterns.logic:
1. Direct Task Manager = **Ctrl+Shift+Esc**.
2. Ctrl+Alt+Del opens the **security screen** first (Lock, Switch user, Sign out, Task Manager).
3. Alt+F4 closes the active program; it does not open Task Manager.

example.q: Which combination opens **Task Manager directly**, without any intermediate screen?
example.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+Esc** — Ctrl+Alt+Del first shows the security menu, from which Task Manager is one more click away.

patterns.name: File Explorer shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Shortcut to create a new folder', 'which key renames a file?', 'properties of a file with keyboard', 'move up one folder'.
patterns.logic:
1. New folder = **Ctrl+Shift+N** (in Explorer; in a browser the same combo makes an Incognito window — classic cross-app trap).
2. F2 = rename, Alt+Enter = properties, Alt+Up = parent folder, Shift+Delete = permanent delete.
3. Ordinary Delete goes to the Recycle Bin; the Shift version skips it.

example.q: In File Explorer, the keyboard shortcut to create a **new folder** is —
example.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N**. (The same combo in Chrome opens an Incognito window — read which app the stem names.)

patterns.name: Window switching and closing
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which combination switches between open windows?', 'closing the active program', 'snapping a window to half the screen'.
patterns.logic:
1. Switch = **Alt+Tab**; close the active program = **Alt+F4**; close a document/tab inside a program = Ctrl+W or Ctrl+F4.
2. Snap = Win+arrow keys (left/right halves, up maximise, down restore/minimise).
3. Shift+Alt+Tab walks the switcher backwards — a rare but asked variant.

example.q: Which key combination **closes the active program window**?
example.solution: **Alt+F4** — it closes the program in front. Alt+Tab only switches between programs; Ctrl+W closes the current document or tab inside them.

subtopics.title: Universal Ctrl keys and MS Word shortcuts
subtopics.concept:
**Universal Ctrl keys** (work in almost every Windows app):

| Key | Action | Key | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ctrl+N | New file | Ctrl+O | Open |
| Ctrl+S | Save | Ctrl+P | Print |
| Ctrl+Z | Undo | Ctrl+Y | Redo / repeat |
| Ctrl+X / C / V | Cut / copy / paste | Ctrl+A | Select all |
| Ctrl+F | Find | Ctrl+W | Close document/tab |

**MS Word:**

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+B / I / U | Bold / italic / underline |
| Ctrl+Shift+D | Double underline |
| Ctrl+L / E / R / J | Align left / centre / right / justify |
| Ctrl+1 / Ctrl+2 / Ctrl+5 | Single / double / 1.5 line spacing |
| Ctrl+] / Ctrl+[ | Font size +1 / -1 point |
| Ctrl+Shift+> / < | Next / previous size in the font list |
| Ctrl+D | Font dialog box |
| Ctrl+Shift+A / Ctrl+Shift+K | ALL CAPS / Small Caps |
| Shift+F3 | Change case (cycles) |
| Ctrl+= / Ctrl+Shift+= | Subscript / superscript |
| Ctrl+Space / Ctrl+Q | Remove character / paragraph formatting |
| Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V | Copy / paste formatting only |
| Ctrl+H / Ctrl+G (or F5) | Replace / Go To |
| Ctrl+K | Insert hyperlink |
| Ctrl+Enter | Page break |
| Ctrl+M / Ctrl+Shift+M | Increase / decrease indent |
| Ctrl+T | Hanging indent |
| Ctrl+Alt+1/2/3 | Heading 1/2/3 style |
| Ctrl+Shift+8 | Show/hide formatting marks (the pilcrow) |
| Alt+Shift+D / Alt+Shift+T | Insert date / time |
| Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End | Start / end of the document |
| Ctrl+F2 | Print preview |
| Ctrl+F1 | Collapse/expand the ribbon |
| Alt+Ctrl+F / Alt+Ctrl+D | Footnote / endnote |
| F7 / Shift+F7 | Spelling and grammar / thesaurus |
| Ctrl+Shift+G | Word count |
| F12 | Save As |

tricks.title: L-E-R-J alignment
tricks.body: **L**eft, c**E**ntre, **R**ight, **J**ustify. C is already taken by Copy, so centre borrows the E from cEntre.

example.q: Shortcut to centre a heading in Word?
example.solution: Ctrl+E.

tricks.title: Spacing = the number itself
tricks.body: Ctrl+1 gives single spacing, Ctrl+2 gives double, and Ctrl+5 gives 1.5. Five is the odd one out: read it as 1.5.

example.q: Ctrl+5 in Word sets?
example.solution: 1.5 line spacing.

mistakes: Using Ctrl+C for centre - Ctrl+C copies; centre is Ctrl+E.
Thinking Ctrl+D is 'duplicate' in Word - in Word it opens the Font dialog (duplicate is PowerPoint).
Confusing Ctrl+H: Replace in Word, but History in a web browser.
subtopics.notes:
### The universal Ctrl keys (every Windows app)
| Key | Action | Key | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ctrl+N** | New file | **Ctrl+O** | Open |
| **Ctrl+S** | Save | **Ctrl+P** | Print |
| **Ctrl+Z** | **Undo** | **Ctrl+Y** | Redo |
| **Ctrl+X** | Cut | **Ctrl+C** | Copy |
| **Ctrl+V** | Paste | **Ctrl+A** | Select all |
| **Ctrl+F** | Find | **Ctrl+W** | Close document/tab |
| **Ctrl+K** | Insert hyperlink | **Ctrl+B/I/U** | Bold / italic / underline |

Letter logic: X looks like scissors (cut), V is a paste-down arrow, Z takes you back (undo), A = all.

### Formatting keys (Word especially)
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+B / I / U | Bold / italic / underline |
| **Ctrl+L / E / R / J** | Align **L**eft / c**E**ntre / **R**ight / **J**ustify |
| **Ctrl+1 / Ctrl+2 / Ctrl+5** | Single / double / 1.5 line spacing |
| Ctrl+Shift+D | Double underline |
| Shift+F3 | Cycle CASE (lower → UPPER → Capitalise) |

Memory hooks: **C is taken by Copy, so centre borrows E** ('cEntre'). Spacing uses the number itself — 1 single, 2 double — and 5 is the odd one for 1.5.

### Find, replace, go to
- **Ctrl+F** — Find (in Word it opens the Navigation pane; in browsers 'find in page').
- **Ctrl+H** — **Replace** in Word/Excel (but History in a browser — a favourite cross-app trap).
- **Ctrl+G** and **F5** — Go To a page/line in Word.
- **Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End** — jump to the start / end of the document.

### Undo and friends
- **Ctrl+Z** undoes the last action (press again to undo more); **Ctrl+Y** redoes it.
- Ctrl+S saves — press often; **F12** is Save As (Office).

### The double-life table (same key, different app)
| Key | Word / Excel | Browser | Explorer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ctrl+H | **Replace** | History | — |
| Ctrl+D | Font dialog / fill down | **Bookmark** | — |
| Ctrl+Shift+N | — | Incognito window | **New folder** |
| Ctrl+F | Find (Navigation pane) | Find on page | Search box |
| Ctrl+W | Close document | Close tab | Close window |

How the exam uses it: the stem names the app in italics or bold — "in **MS Word**", "in a **web browser**". Read that phrase before anything else; it flips half the answers in this topic.

Worked example: "In MS Excel, pressing Ctrl+D will —" → fill down (copy the cell above). The same keys in Word open the Font dialog, and in Chrome they bookmark the page. One key, three lives, and only the stem's app decides.

### Quick revision
- N-O-S-P: New, Open, Save, Print. X-C-V: cut-copy-paste. Z-Y: undo-redo.
- Alignment LERJ: Left, cEntre, Right, Justify. Spacing: 1-2-5 = single-double-1.5.
- Ctrl+F find, Ctrl+H replace (Word) but history (browser). Ctrl+K hyperlink.
- Ctrl+Home/Ctrl+End = document start/end. F12 = Save As in Office.

patterns.name: Universal Ctrl-key recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which shortcut pastes / cuts / undoes / selects all?' — the everyday edit keys.
patterns.logic:
1. Edit trio: Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+V paste; Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo; Ctrl+A select all.
2. File quartet: Ctrl+N new, Ctrl+O open, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+P print.
3. Memory hooks: X = scissors, V = paste-down, Z = back. Eliminate combos using Win or Alt where the stem says Ctrl.

example.q: Which shortcut **undoes** the last action in almost every Windows program?
example.solution: **Ctrl+Z** — Z walks you back; Ctrl+Y redoes what you undid.

patterns.name: Formatting keys (bold, align, spacing, case)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which shortcut justifies text?', 'double line spacing', 'which key makes text bold?', 'Shift+F3 does what?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Bold/italic/underline = Ctrl+B/I/U. Alignments = Ctrl+L/E/R/J (LERJ: Left, cEntre, Right, Justify).
2. Line spacing = the number itself: Ctrl+1 single, Ctrl+2 double, Ctrl+5 = 1.5.
3. Shift+F3 cycles the case of selected text in Word.

example.q: Which shortcut sets **double line spacing** on the selected paragraphs in Word?
example.solution: **Ctrl+2** — the number is the spacing itself: Ctrl+1 single, Ctrl+2 double, Ctrl+5 = 1.5 lines.

patterns.name: Find / Replace / Go To / navigation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Shortcut for Find and Replace', 'jump to the beginning of the document', 'which opens the Go To dialog?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+F find, Ctrl+H replace (Word/Excel), Ctrl+G or F5 = Go To (Word).
2. Ctrl+Home jumps to the document start, Ctrl+End to the end.
3. Cross-app trap: Ctrl+H is Replace in Office but History in browsers.

example.q: Which shortcut opens **Find and Replace** directly on the Replace tab in MS Word?
example.solution: **Ctrl+H** — H for 'hunt and swap'. Ctrl+F only finds; F5 or Ctrl+G goes to a page or line.

patterns.name: Trap pairs and reverse recall in Office
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ctrl+D in Word does what?' (Font dialog, not duplicate), 'Ctrl+E in Excel vs Word', statements that swap Replace/History or centre/copy.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+D: **Font dialog in Word**, fill-down in Excel, bookmark in browsers — same key, three lives.
2. Ctrl+E: centre in Word, but 'export' nowhere — in Excel it centres too; beware options inventing actions.
3. Reverse recall: read the action in the stem, then recall the key, then check which app the stem names.

example.q: In **MS Word**, pressing Ctrl+D opens the —
example.solution: **Font dialog box** — not 'duplicate' (that is PowerPoint's Ctrl+D) and not fill-down (that is Excel's).

subtopics.title: MS Excel and PowerPoint shortcuts
subtopics.concept:
**MS Excel:**

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End | Go to A1 / last used cell |
| Ctrl+Arrow | Jump to the edge of the data region |
| Ctrl+PageDown / Ctrl+PageUp | Next / previous worksheet |
| Ctrl+Space / Shift+Space | Select entire column / row |
| Ctrl+D / Ctrl+R | Fill down / fill right |
| Ctrl+Enter | Fill every selected cell with the same entry |
| Ctrl+; / Ctrl+Shift+; | Insert current date / time |
| Alt+= | AutoSum |
| Alt+Enter | New line inside a cell |
| F2 | Edit active cell |
| F4 | Cycle \$ reference types (or repeat last action) |
| Shift+F3 | Insert Function dialog |
| F9 | Recalculate all workbooks |
| F11 / Alt+F1 | Chart on a new chart sheet / embedded chart |
| Shift+F11 | Insert new worksheet |
| Ctrl+1 | Format Cells dialog |
| Ctrl+Shift+\$ / % / # | Currency / percentage / date format |
| Ctrl+9 / Ctrl+0 | Hide rows / hide columns |
| Ctrl+- / Ctrl+Shift++ | Delete / insert cells |
| Ctrl+T | Create a table |
| Ctrl+E | Flash Fill |
| Ctrl+Shift+L | Toggle filter |
| Ctrl+` | Show formulas instead of results |

**MS PowerPoint:** F5 show from slide 1; Shift+F5 show from the current slide; Esc ends the show; B/W black/white screen; N/P next/previous; number+Enter jumps to a slide; Ctrl+P pen and E erases ink during a show; Ctrl+M new slide; Ctrl+D duplicate; Alt+F5 presenter view.

tricks.title: Same key, different app
tricks.body: **Shift+F3**: change case in Word, Insert Function in Excel. **Ctrl+D**: Font dialog in Word, fill down in Excel, duplicate in PowerPoint, bookmark in a browser. **F5**: Go To in Word/Excel, slide show in PowerPoint, refresh in a browser. Always read which application the question names.

example.q: Shift+F3 in MS Excel opens?
example.solution: The Insert Function dialog (not change case).

tricks.title: Page keys move pages (sheets)
tricks.body: In Excel, Ctrl+PageDown moves to the next sheet and Ctrl+PageUp to the previous one, as if turning pages of the workbook.

example.q: Move to the previous worksheet?
example.solution: Ctrl+PageUp.

mistakes: Choosing Ctrl+Shift+; for the date - that inserts the time; the date is Ctrl+;.
Answering F11 for 'insert worksheet' - F11 makes a chart sheet; Shift+F11 inserts a worksheet.
subtopics.notes:
### Excel: moving around
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Home** | Jump to cell **A1** |
| **Ctrl+End** | Jump to the last used cell |
| **Ctrl+Page Down / Up** | Next / previous **worksheet** |
| **Ctrl+Arrow key** | Edge of the current data region |
| **F5 / Ctrl+G** | Go To a named cell |
| **Ctrl+F** | Find |

### Excel: selecting and editing
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Space** | Select the whole **column** |
| **Shift+Space** | Select the whole **row** |
| **Ctrl+A** | Select the worksheet/data region |
| **F2** | **Edit** the active cell (also double-click) |
| **Alt+Enter** | New **line inside a cell** |
| **Ctrl+D** | **Fill down** from the cell above |
| **Ctrl+R** | **Fill right** from the cell on the left |
| **Ctrl+;** | Insert today's **date** |
| **Ctrl+Shift+;** | Insert the current **time** |
| **F4** | Cycle absolute and relative references; repeat last action |
| Ctrl+1 | Format Cells dialog |
| Ctrl+Shift+L | Toggle AutoFilter |
| Alt+= | AutoSum |
| Shift+F11 | New worksheet |

Memory hooks: **Ctrl+Space = one column tall and thin; Shift+Space = one row flat.** The **semicolon** gives the timestamp pair — plain ; is date, with Shift it is time (': ' shares the key, time is the shifted thing).

### PowerPoint: running the show
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **F5** | Start the slideshow from the **beginning** |
| **Shift+F5** | Start from the **current slide** |
| **Esc** | End the slideshow |
| **B** | Black screen (press again to return); **W** = white screen |
| **N / Space / Right** | Next slide; **P / Left** = previous |
| number + Enter | Jump to that slide number |
| **Ctrl+M** | New slide |
| Ctrl+D | Duplicate the current slide |

Trap set: Ctrl+D **duplicates** a slide in PowerPoint but **fills down** in Excel and opens the **Font dialog** in Word — the same key with three jobs.

### Everyday anchors and worked pairs
| You want to… | Press |
|---|---|
| Put "Total" under every month's column | Type once, then Ctrl+D down the column |
| Jump to the last cell you ever filled | Ctrl+End |
| Type an address over two lines in one cell | Alt+Enter between the lines |
| Stamp today's date on a report | Ctrl+; |
| Check one slide without running the whole deck | Shift+F5 |
| Keep the audience looking at you, not the slide | B (black) during the show |

Ten-second method: the stem gives an action ("select the row", "fill down", "start the show") → recall the family (selection = Space pair, filling = D/R, show = F5/Shift+F5) → eliminate options that swap row/column or F5/Shift+F5.

### Quick revision
- Excel corners: Ctrl+Home → A1, Ctrl+End → last cell; sheets via Ctrl+PgDn/PgUp.
- Whole column Ctrl+Space, whole row Shift+Space; F2 edits, Alt+Enter breaks a line.
- Fill down D, fill right R; date Ctrl+;, time Ctrl+Shift+;.
- Show: F5 from start, Shift+F5 from here, Esc to stop, B black, W white, Ctrl+M new slide.

patterns.name: Excel navigation shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ctrl+Home in Excel takes you to…', 'jump to the last cell', 'move to the next worksheet'.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+Home = **A1**, Ctrl+End = last used cell — corner recall.
2. Worksheets: Ctrl+PgDn next, Ctrl+PgUp previous.
3. Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the data edge; F5 opens Go To.

example.q: In MS Excel, Ctrl+Home moves the cursor to:
example.solution: Cell **A1** — the home of every worksheet. Ctrl+End goes the other way, to the last used cell.

patterns.name: Row/column selection shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Select the entire column', 'select the whole row', 'which selects the entire sheet?' — the Space pair.
patterns.logic:
1. **Ctrl+Space = column, Shift+Space = row**; Ctrl+A = whole sheet.
2. Trap: options swap the two, or offer plain Space (which just extends selection by a cell in some modes).
3. Anchor line: 'Control the column, Shift the row.'

example.q: Which shortcut selects the **entire column** of the active cell in Excel?
example.solution: **Ctrl+Space** — 'Control the column'; Shift+Space selects the entire row instead.

patterns.name: Excel editing and data-entry shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Edit the contents of a cell', 'enter a new line within a cell', 'fill down', 'insert current date with a shortcut'.
patterns.logic:
1. F2 edits the cell; Alt+Enter puts a line break inside it; Ctrl+D fills down, Ctrl+R fills right.
2. Ctrl+; stamps today's date; Ctrl+Shift+; stamps the time.
3. F4 cycles dollar signs in a formula (and repeats the last action).

example.q: Which key **edits the contents of the active cell** in Excel?
example.solution: **F2** — it turns the cell into edit mode (the same as double-clicking it).

patterns.name: PowerPoint slideshow shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Start the slide show from the beginning', 'shortcut to end a presentation', 'black screen during a show', 'new slide shortcut'.
patterns.logic:
1. F5 = show from slide 1; **Shift+F5 = from the current slide**; Esc = end the show.
2. B black / W white (press again to come back); N or Space = next; P = previous.
3. Ctrl+M inserts a new slide; Ctrl+D duplicates the current one.

example.q: The shortcut to run a PowerPoint presentation **from the beginning** is:
example.solution: **F5** — full show. Shift+F5 starts from whichever slide you are on.

subtopics.title: Web browser shortcuts (Chrome, Edge, Firefox)
subtopics.concept:
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+T / Ctrl+W | New tab / close tab |
| Ctrl+Shift+T | Reopen the last closed tab |
| Ctrl+N | New window |
| Ctrl+Shift+N | Incognito (Chrome) / InPrivate (Edge) window |
| Ctrl+Shift+P | Private window in Firefox |
| Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+Tab | Next / previous tab |
| Ctrl+1 ... Ctrl+8 / Ctrl+9 | Jump to tab 1-8 / last tab |
| Alt+Left / Alt+Right | Back / forward |
| Alt+Home | Home page |
| Ctrl+D | Bookmark the current page |
| Ctrl+Shift+B | Show/hide the bookmarks (favourites) bar |
| Ctrl+H / Ctrl+J | History / downloads |
| Ctrl+Shift+Delete | Clear browsing data |
| F5 or Ctrl+R / Ctrl+F5 | Reload / hard reload (skip cache) |
| Esc | Stop loading the page |
| Ctrl+L, Alt+D or F6 | Select the address bar |
| Ctrl+F, then F3 | Find on page, then find next |
| Ctrl++ / Ctrl+- / Ctrl+0 | Zoom in / zoom out / reset zoom |
| Ctrl+U | View page source |
| F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I | Developer tools |
| F11 | Full screen |
| Ctrl+Enter (in address bar) | Adds www. and .com around a typed word |

tricks.title: Shift = undo the tab
tricks.body: Ctrl+T opens a tab and **Ctrl+Shift+T** brings back the one you closed. Shift adds 'the opposite' or 'the stronger version': Ctrl+Shift+N is a stronger (private) new window, and Ctrl+Shift+Delete is a stronger delete (all browsing data).

example.q: You closed a tab by mistake. Shortcut to restore it?
example.solution: Ctrl+Shift+T.

tricks.title: Alt+arrows = time travel
tricks.body: Alt+Left goes back in history and Alt+Right goes forward. Backspace no longer goes back in Chrome.

example.q: Go back to the previous page?
example.solution: Alt+Left arrow.

mistakes: Saying Ctrl+Shift+N opens a private window in Firefox - Firefox uses Ctrl+Shift+P.
Thinking Ctrl+W closes the whole browser - it closes only the current tab.
subtopics.notes:
### Tabs
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+T** | New tab |
| **Ctrl+W** (Ctrl+F4) | Close the current tab |
| **Ctrl+Shift+T** | **Reopen the last closed tab** — the undo of Ctrl+W |
| **Ctrl+Tab** | Next tab; Ctrl+Shift+Tab = previous |
| **Ctrl+1…8** | Jump to tab number 1–8 |
| **Ctrl+9** | Jump to the **last** tab (not number 9) |

### Windows and privacy
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+N** | New window |
| **Ctrl+Shift+N** | New **Incognito/Private** window (Chrome/Edge) |
| **Ctrl+Shift+P** | Private window in **Firefox** (in Edge/Chrome it prints) |
| **Ctrl+Shift+Delete** | Open **Clear browsing data** |

### Getting around
| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| **Alt+Left / Alt+Right** | Back / forward |
| **Alt+Home** | Open the home page |
| **F5** | Reload; Ctrl+F5 = reload ignoring cache |
| **F11** | Full screen on/off |
| **Ctrl+F** | Find on the page |
| **Ctrl+D** | **Bookmark** this page |
| **Ctrl+Shift+B** | Show/hide the bookmarks bar |
| **Ctrl+H** | **History** |
| **Ctrl+J** | **Downloads** |

### The Ctrl+H / Ctrl+N / Ctrl+D double lives
The same keys do different things in a browser than in Word/Excel:

| Key | Browser | Word / Excel |
|---|---|---|
| Ctrl+H | **History** | Replace (Word) |
| Ctrl+N | New **window** | New **document/workbook** |
| Ctrl+Shift+N | Incognito window | New **folder** (Explorer) |
| Ctrl+D | **Bookmark** | Font dialog (Word) / fill down (Excel) |
| Ctrl+F | Find on page | Find (same idea) |

Read the stem: **'in a web browser'** changes the answer.

### Everyday anchors and worked pairs
| You just… | Do this |
|---|---|
| Closed a tab you still needed | Ctrl+Shift+T brings it back |
| Want a second, separate browsing session | Ctrl+N (normal) or Ctrl+Shift+N (private) |
| Filled a form and want nothing saved | Ctrl+Shift+N / Ctrl+Shift+P window |
| Lost the bookmarks bar | Ctrl+Shift+B |
| Need the page you visited last Tuesday | Ctrl+H |
| Want the installer you downloaded | Ctrl+J |
| Page stuck on an old version | F5 (Ctrl+F5 to bypass cache) |
| Text too small on a crowded page | Ctrl+F to jump straight to the word |

Privacy fact the exams like: Incognito/Private mode stops the browser from **saving history and cookies locally** on that computer — it does not hide your activity from websites, employers or internet providers.

### Quick revision
- Tab trio: T new, W close, Shift+T reopen. Ctrl+9 = last tab, not the 9th.
- Private: Ctrl+Shift+N (Chrome/Edge), Ctrl+Shift+P (Firefox). Clear data: Ctrl+Shift+Delete.
- Back/forward = Alt+Left/Right; home = Alt+Home; full screen = F11.
- Bookmarks Ctrl+D, history Ctrl+H, downloads Ctrl+J.

patterns.name: Browser tab management
patterns.howToSpot: 'Open a new tab', 'reopen the accidentally closed tab', 'switch tabs with keyboard', 'close the current tab'.
patterns.logic:
1. Trio: Ctrl+**T** new, Ctrl+**W** close, Ctrl+**Shift+T** reopen closed.
2. Switch: Ctrl+Tab next, Ctrl+Shift+Tab previous, Ctrl+1-8 numbered tabs.
3. Ctrl+9 is the **last** tab, not the ninth — a classic twist.

example.q: You closed a browser tab by mistake. Which shortcut brings it **back**?
example.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+T** reopens the most recently closed tab (press repeatedly to walk back through them).

patterns.name: Private/incognito windows
patterns.howToSpot: 'Shortcut for Incognito/Private mode', 'which browser uses Ctrl+Shift+P?', 'new window vs new tab'.
patterns.logic:
1. Chrome/Edge private = **Ctrl+Shift+N**; Firefox private = **Ctrl+Shift+P**.
2. Plain Ctrl+N = new ordinary window — not private.
3. Incognito does not make you anonymous; it just avoids saving history/cookies locally (exam phrasing: 'not recorded in browsing history').

example.q: Which shortcut opens an **Incognito window** in Google Chrome?
example.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N** — N for the new, untracked window. (Firefox's private window uses Ctrl+Shift+P.)

patterns.name: Browser navigation and bookmarks
patterns.howToSpot: 'Go back to the previous page', 'open the home page', 'bookmark a page with the keyboard', 'show the bookmarks bar'.
patterns.logic:
1. Back/forward = **Alt+Left / Alt+Right**; home page = Alt+Home; full screen = F11.
2. Bookmark = Ctrl+D; toggle the bookmarks bar = Ctrl+Shift+B.
3. Reload = F5; find on page = Ctrl+F.

example.q: In a web browser, which shortcut takes you **back to the previous page**?
example.solution: **Alt+Left arrow** (Backspace also worked historically, but the exam answer is Alt+Left). Alt+Right goes forward.

patterns.name: History, downloads and clearing data
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ctrl+H opens…', 'shortcut to open downloads', 'shortcut that opens the clear-browsing-data dialog'.
patterns.logic:
1. **H = History, J = 'get list' → Downloads, Ctrl+Shift+Delete = Clear browsing data.**
2. Trap: Ctrl+H in Word is Replace — read whether the stem says browser.
3. Delete in the clear-data combo is the permanent-delete key — fitting for 'wipe history'.

example.q: In a web browser, **Ctrl+H** opens —
example.solution: **Browsing History** — the list of pages you visited. (In MS Word the same keys open Find and Replace.)

subtopics.title: Function keys F1-F12
subtopics.concept:
| Key | Windows / Explorer | MS Office | Browser |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Help | Help | Help |
| F2 | Rename selected item | Edit active cell (Excel) | - |
| F3 | Search in Explorer | Shift+F3: change case (Word), Insert Function (Excel) | Find next |
| F4 | Alt+F4 closes window; address-bar list in Explorer | Repeat last action; cycle absolute/relative references (Excel) | - |
| F5 | Refresh | Go To (Word/Excel); start slide show (PowerPoint) | Reload |
| F6 | Cycle through screen elements | Move between panes/ribbon | Focus address bar |
| F7 | - | Spelling and grammar; Shift+F7 thesaurus | Caret browsing |
| F8 | Boot options on older PCs | Extend selection (Word/Excel) | - |
| F9 | - | Recalculate (Excel); update field (Word) | - |
| F10 | Activate menu bar; **Shift+F10 = right-click menu** | Show KeyTips | Menu |
| F11 | Full screen | New chart sheet (Excel); Shift+F11 new worksheet | Full screen |
| F12 | - | Save As | Developer tools |

Exam favourites: **F1 Help, F2 Rename/Edit, F5 Refresh/Slide show, F7 Spell check, F12 Save As, Shift+F10 context menu, Alt+F4 close.**

tricks.title: 1-2-5-7-12 ladder
tricks.body: F**1** = help (first thing you need), F**2** = rename (give it a 2nd name), F**5** = refresh/show (5 = S for Show), F**7** = spell check (7 letters in 'SPELLER'), F**12** = Save As (end of the row, you save at the end).

example.q: Which key opens Save As in Word?

tricks.title: Shift+F10 = right-click
tricks.body: Shift+F10 opens the context menu, the same one you get with a right mouse click. The Menu key next to right Ctrl does the same.

example.q: Keyboard equivalent of a right-click?
example.solution: Shift+F10.

mistakes: Answering F2 for 'refresh' - refresh is F5; F2 renames.
Saying F12 saves normally - F12 is Save As; plain save is Ctrl+S.
Treating F11 the same in every app - full screen in browsers, chart sheet in Excel.
subtopics.notes:
### The F1–F12 row, one by one
| Key | Everywhere / Windows | In Office | Elsewhere |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | **Help** | Help | — |
| **F2** | Rename file (Explorer) | Edit cell (Excel) | — |
| **F3** | Search (Explorer) | Insert Function (Shift+F3) | — |
| **F4** | Address-bar dropdown | Repeat last action; cycles absolute refs in formulas | Alt+F4 closes the program |
| **F5** | **Refresh** | Slideshow (PPT) / Go To (Word) | Hard reload Ctrl+F5 |
| **F6** | Cycle screen elements/panes | — | — |
| **F7** | — | **Spelling & grammar** | Caret browsing in browsers |
| **F8** | Safe Mode at start-up (older Windows) | Extend selection | — |
| **F9** | Update fields (Word) | Recalculate | Send/Receive (Outlook) |
| **F10** | Activate the menu bar | — | **Shift+F10 = right-click** |
| **F11** | Full screen (browsers) | Chart sheet (Excel) | — |
| **F12** | Developer tools (browsers) | **Save As** | — |

Memory hooks:
- **One = on-demand help. Two = second name (rename). Five = fresh (refresh). Seven = spellcheck's number. Twelve = twelve dollars — Save As your work.**
- The **Shift+F10 = right-click** rule: F10 summons the menu bar, Shift makes it act where your cursor is — the keyboard's right-click.
- **Alt+F4 closes** the program; **Ctrl+F4 closes only the document/tab** inside it.

### Same key, different apps (the exam's favourite twist)
| Key | Windows | Word | Excel | PowerPoint | Browser |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F5 | Refresh | Go To | Go To | **Slideshow** | Reload |
| F2 | Rename | — | Edit cell | — | — |
| F7 | — | Spellcheck | Spellcheck | Spellcheck | Caret browsing |
| F12 | Dev tools | Save As | Save As | Save As | Dev tools |
| F11 | — | Full screen (Alt) | Chart sheet | — | Full screen |

The stem names the app — **F5 in PowerPoint is the show, F5 on the desktop is refresh**.

### Everyday anchors and worked pairs
| You want to… | Press |
|---|---|
| Understand a button you have never clicked | F1 |
| Give a file a better name | F2 |
| Search a folder full of files | F3 |
| Reload a page that misbehaves | F5 |
| Fix every red squiggle at once | F7 |
| Send the file with a different name | F12 |
| Open the menu without the mouse | F10 (Shift+F10 = right-click menu) |

Ten-second method: the stem gives an action → say the ladder out loud ("help, rename, search, refresh, …") and stop at the match → then check the app named, because F5 and F12 change jobs between Office and the browser.

### Quick revision
- F1 help, F2 rename/edit, F3 search, F5 refresh/show, F7 spelling, F12 save-as/dev-tools.
- Alt+F4 close program; Ctrl+F4 close document; Shift+F10 = right-click; F10 = menu bar.
- F4 repeats the last action (Office) and cycles absolute/relative references (Excel); F8 = Safe Mode at boot (older Windows).
- Shift+F3 toggles case in Word; Shift+F11 adds a worksheet; Ctrl+F5 = reload without cache.

patterns.name: Core F-key identification
patterns.howToSpot: 'F1 is used for…', 'which function key refreshes the page?', 'which key is pressed to rename a file?', 'save-as key'.
patterns.logic:
1. Ladder recall: **F1 help → F2 rename/edit → F3 search → F5 refresh → F7 spelling → F12 save-as.**
2. Anchor each with a hook: one = on-demand help, five = fresh, twelve = save.
3. Check the app named in the stem before locking F5 or F12.

example.q: Which function key **refreshes** the active window or web page?
example.solution: **F5** — the refresh/reload key everywhere on Windows.

patterns.name: F-keys inside Office apps
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which key runs the spell check?', 'which key starts the slideshow?', 'Shift+F3 does what in Word?', 'Shift+F11 inserts…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Office ladder: F2 edit cell (Excel), F4 repeat/absolute refs, F5 show (PPT)/Go To (Word), F7 spelling, F12 Save As.
2. Shift variants: Shift+F3 case (Word), Shift+F5 show from current slide, Shift+F11 new worksheet (Excel), Shift+F10 right-click.
3. The app decides: F5 in PowerPoint = show, F5 in Word = Go To.

example.q: Which function key runs **Spelling & Grammar check** in MS Word?
example.solution: **F7** — the spellchecker's key in Word, Excel and PowerPoint alike.

patterns.name: Modifier + F-key combinations
patterns.howToSpot: 'Alt+F4 does what?', 'which combination works like right-click?', 'Ctrl+F4 vs Alt+F4', 'Shift+F10 opens'.
patterns.logic:
1. Alt+F4 closes the whole program; Ctrl+F4 closes only the open document/tab inside it.
2. Shift+F10 = the context (right-click) menu; F10 alone activates the menu bar.
3. Alt+Enter = properties of a file; Alt+Tab = switch windows.

example.q: Which key combination works like a **right-click** (opens the shortcut menu)?
example.solution: **Shift+F10** — it opens the context menu at the current selection, no mouse needed.

patterns.name: One key, many apps (application-dependent F-keys)
patterns.howToSpot: 'In PowerPoint F5 does what but on the desktop?', 'F12 in a browser vs in Word', 'F11 in Excel vs in a browser', 'which is NOT true about F-keys'.
patterns.logic:
1. Build the cross-table: F5 = refresh (Windows/browser) vs slideshow (PPT) vs Go To (Word/Excel).
2. F12 = Save As (Office) vs developer tools (browsers). F11 = full screen (browser) vs chart sheet (Excel).
3. Statement questions: verify each clause against the right app before judging true/false.

example.q: Which statement about the function keys is **correct**?
example.solution: F12 has two lives: **Save As** in Office apps, **developer tools** in browsers. F5 shows slides in PowerPoint and refreshes elsewhere; F11 is full screen in browsers, a chart sheet in Excel.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which shortcut opens File Explorer / creates a new folder / locks the screen?', 'the shortcut to close the active program is'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall by first-letter logic on the Win-key row (Win+E Explorer, Win+L Lock, Win+R Run) and by family: Alt+F4 closes a program, Alt+Tab switches, Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager directly while Ctrl+Alt+Del shows the security screen first. Eliminate options whose modifier contradicts the verb.

example.q: Which shortcut opens File Explorer?
example.solution: Win+E — E for Explorer. Win+X is the power-user menu, Win+P projection.

pyqPatterns.pattern: 'What does key X do' reverse recall
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Ctrl+H in Word opens…', 'Ctrl+D in Word/Excel does what?', 'What is the function of Ctrl+Y?' — the key is given, the action is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Reverse the table: key first, then app. Ctrl+H = Replace in Word but History in a browser; Ctrl+D = Font dialog in Word, fill down in Excel, duplicate in PowerPoint, bookmark in a browser; Ctrl+Y = redo. Always read which application the stem names before answering.

example.q: In MS Word, Ctrl+D opens the:
example.solution: Font dialog box — not duplicate (PowerPoint) and not fill-down (Excel).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'F1 is used for', 'which key refreshes the page?', 'spell check runs on which function key?', 'which F-key starts the slideshow?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ladder recall: F1 help, F2 rename/edit cell, F3 search, F5 refresh/show/Go To, F7 spelling, F12 Save As (Office) or developer tools (browser). Then let the app decide: F5 in PowerPoint is the show, F5 on the desktop is refresh.

example.q: Which function key runs the spelling and grammar check?
example.solution: F7 — in Word, Excel and PowerPoint alike.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'F5 in MS PowerPoint starts… but on the desktop it…', 'Ctrl+D has different uses in Word, Excel and a browser', statement questions mixing apps.
pyqPatterns.approach: Build the cross-table: F5 = refresh/reload (Windows, browsers) vs slideshow (PPT) vs Go To (Word); F12 = Save As (Office) vs dev tools (browser); Ctrl+Shift+N = Incognito (browser) vs new folder (Explorer); Ctrl+H = Replace (Word) vs History (browser). The app named in the stem picks the answer.

example.q: F5 in MS PowerPoint starts the slideshow. What does F5 do on the Windows desktop?
example.solution: It refreshes the desktop or active window — same key, different job per application.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Ctrl+H in a browser opens…', 'shortcut for Incognito mode', 'which shortcut reopens a closed tab?', 'Ctrl+D in Chrome does what?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Browser column: Ctrl+T new tab, Ctrl+W close, Ctrl+Shift+T reopen closed, Ctrl+Shift+N Incognito (Firefox = Ctrl+Shift+P), Alt+Left back, Ctrl+D bookmark, Ctrl+H history, Ctrl+J downloads, Ctrl+Shift+Delete clear data. Check the stem says 'browser' — Ctrl+H is Replace in Word and Ctrl+Shift+N is a new folder in Explorer.

example.q: In a web browser, Ctrl+H opens:
example.solution: Browsing history — the same keys open Find and Replace in MS Word.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: List A has shortcuts (or keys), List B has actions; options are four mappings like 'A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Solve the sure pairs first: bold Ctrl+B, undo Ctrl+Z, Task Manager Ctrl+Shift+Esc, new folder Ctrl+Shift+N, slideshow F5. Strike every option mispairing a certain pair, then match the leftovers by elimination.

example.q:
Match: A. Ctrl+Shift+N  B. Alt+F4  C. Win+E  D. Ctrl+Shift+Esc
1. Close program 2. New folder 3. Task Manager 4. File Explorer
example.solution: A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3 — each certain pair removes two wrong options at once.

solvedExamples.q: Which Windows shortcut locks the computer immediately, so a password or PIN is needed to return?
solvedExamples.solution: Win+L locks the workstation and shows the lock screen. Win+D shows the desktop and Win+M minimises all windows, but neither locks anything. Ctrl+Alt+L is not a Windows lock key.

solvedExamples.q: Pressing Shift+F10 in Windows has the same effect as:
solvedExamples.solution: Shift+F10 opens the shortcut (context) menu for the selected item, exactly like a right mouse click. F10 on its own activates the menu bar.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Shift+F10 = right-click; F10 alone = menu bar.

solvedExamples.q: In MS Excel, which shortcut moves to the NEXT worksheet in the workbook?
solvedExamples.solution: Ctrl+PageDown moves to the next sheet and Ctrl+PageUp to the previous one. Shift+F11 inserts a new worksheet rather than moving to one. Ctrl+Tab switches between open workbooks.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Page keys turn the workbook's pages: Down = next, Up = previous.

solvedExamples.q: In MS Word, Excel and PowerPoint, the F12 key opens the:
solvedExamples.solution: F12 opens Save As in all Office apps. Ctrl+P prints, F1 opens Help and F7 runs the spelling check.
solvedExamples.shortcut: F12 is at the end of the row, and you Save As at the end of your work.

practice.q: Which shortcut minimises all open windows to show the desktop, and restores them when pressed again?
practice.solution: Win+D toggles the desktop: the first press hides every window and the second press brings them back. Win+E opens File Explorer, and Win+Tab/Alt+Tab switch windows.

practice.q: In Windows 10/11, pressing Win+V opens:
practice.solution: Win+V shows clipboard history, a list of recently copied items you can paste again (it must be switched on the first time). Run is Win+R and voice typing is Win+H.
practice.shortcut: Ctrl+V pastes one item; Win+V opens the whole paste history.

practice.q: Which shortcut lets you drag a box to capture a chosen part of the screen with the Snipping Tool?
practice.solution: Win+Shift+S opens the screen snip toolbar (rectangle, free-form, window, full screen). Alt+PrtScn captures only the active window, Win+P changes display projection, and Ctrl+Shift+S is Save As in some apps.
practice.shortcut: S = Snip; Win+Shift makes it a system-wide snip.

practice.q: Which key combination switches between open application windows?
practice.solution: Alt+Tab cycles through all open windows. Ctrl+Tab switches tabs inside one application, Shift+Tab moves focus backwards, and Alt+F4 closes the window.
practice.shortcut: Alt = Active window: Alt+Tab switches it, Alt+F4 closes it.

practice.q: The Run dialog box, used to launch programs such as 'cmd' or 'calc' by name, opens with:
practice.solution: Win+R opens Run. Win+X opens the Quick Link (power user) menu. Ctrl+R reloads a browser page and does Fill Right in Excel.

practice.q: In Windows File Explorer, which shortcut creates a new folder in the current location?
practice.solution: Ctrl+Shift+N creates a new folder in Explorer. Plain Ctrl+N opens a new Explorer window. In Chrome, Ctrl+Shift+N opens an incognito window.
practice.shortcut: Ctrl+N = new window; add Shift for a new folder.

practice.q: A file is selected in File Explorer. Pressing Alt+Enter will:
practice.solution: Alt+Enter opens the Properties dialog (size, location, dates, attributes). Enter opens the file, F2 renames it and Delete sends it to the Recycle Bin.

practice.q: In MS Word, Ctrl+J applies which alignment to the selected paragraph?
practice.solution: Ctrl+J justifies text so both margins are straight. Left is Ctrl+L, centre is Ctrl+E and right is Ctrl+R.

practice.q: Which shortcut sets double line spacing in MS Word?
practice.solution: Ctrl+2 gives double spacing, Ctrl+1 single spacing and Ctrl+5 1.5 spacing. Ctrl+D opens the Font dialog.
practice.shortcut: The digit is the spacing; 5 means 1.5.

practice.q: The Find and Replace dialog in MS Word opens directly on the Replace tab with:
practice.solution: Ctrl+H opens Replace. Ctrl+F opens the Navigation (find) pane, Ctrl+G opens Go To, and Ctrl+R right-aligns text.
practice.shortcut: H = cHange/replace in Word (but History in a browser).

practice.q: In MS Excel, pressing Ctrl+Space selects:
practice.solution: Ctrl+Space selects the whole column of the active cell and Shift+Space selects the whole row. Ctrl+A selects the data region, or the whole sheet if pressed again.
practice.shortcut: Ctrl and Column both start with C; Shift+Space = row.

practice.q: A value is in A2 and the range A2:A10 is selected. Which shortcut copies A2 into A3:A10?
practice.solution: Ctrl+D (Fill Down) copies the top cell of the selection into the cells below it. Ctrl+R fills right, Ctrl+C only copies to the clipboard, and Ctrl+E is Flash Fill.

practice.q: In MS Excel, the shortcut Shift+F3 opens the:
practice.solution: In Excel, Shift+F3 opens Insert Function (the fx dialog). The change-case meaning belongs to MS Word, which is the trap. Name Manager is Ctrl+F3.
practice.shortcut: Same key, different app: Word = case, Excel = function.

practice.q: In Chrome and Edge, which shortcut opens the 'Clear browsing data' dialog?
practice.solution: Ctrl+Shift+Delete opens the dialog for clearing history, cookies and cached files. Shift+Delete is permanent file deletion in File Explorer, not a browser command.
practice.shortcut: Ctrl+Shift = the strong version; the strongest delete wipes browsing data.

practice.q: Which shortcut takes a web browser back to the previously visited page?
practice.solution: Alt+Left goes back and Alt+Right goes forward. Alt+Home opens the home page, and Ctrl+Left moves the cursor one word left in a text box.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens **File Explorer**?
practice.solution: **Win+E** opens File Explorer (E for Explorer). Win+X opens the power-user menu; Win+P handles projection.

practice.q: The **Run** dialog, where you can type 'cmd' or 'calc', opens with —
practice.solution: **Win+R** = Run — type a program name and press Enter.

practice.q: Pressing **Win+D** and then pressing it again will —
options: Show the desktop, then restore the open windows
practice.solution: **Win+D toggles**: first press hides all windows to show the desktop, second press brings them back. Win+M, by contrast, only minimises.

practice.q: Which shortcut captures a **selected part of the screen** with the Snipping overlay?
practice.solution: **Win+Shift+S** opens the snip bar — drag to capture a rectangle, window or full screen.

practice.q: Windows **clipboard history**, which remembers several recent copied items, opens with —
practice.solution: **Win+V** shows the clipboard history (paste any of your recent copies). Plain Ctrl+V pastes only the latest item.

practice.q: Which key combination opens **Task Manager directly**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+Esc** jumps straight to Task Manager. Ctrl+Alt+Del first shows the security screen.
practice.shortcut: Esc = escape straight into Task Manager.

practice.q: Pressing **Ctrl+Alt+Del** shows —
options: The Windows security screen (Lock, Switch user, Sign out, Task Manager)
practice.solution: Ctrl+Alt+Del opens the **security screen**; Task Manager is one option on it. For the direct route, use Ctrl+Shift+Esc.
practice.shortcut: Three keys, one menu, then your pick.

practice.q: In File Explorer, which shortcut creates a **new folder**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N** makes a new folder in the current location. Plain Ctrl+N opens a new window.
practice.shortcut: Shift raises the stakes: window → folder.

practice.q: Which key **renames** a selected file in File Explorer?
practice.solution: **F2** renames the selected item — give it a second name.

practice.q: With a file selected, **Alt+Enter** shows —
options: The file in a new window
practice.solution: **Alt+Enter** opens Properties (size, dates, attributes) — the keyboard way of right-clicking and choosing Properties.

practice.q: You are deep inside C:\Users\Me\Photos\2026. Which shortcut moves **up one folder** (to Photos)?
practice.solution: **Alt+Up** climbs to the parent folder. Alt+Left goes *back* to wherever you came from — not the same thing.
practice.shortcut: Up = one level up; Left = back in history.

practice.q: Which combination **switches between open application windows**?
practice.solution: **Alt+Tab** cycles through open programs (Ctrl+Tab switches tabs inside one app instead).
practice.shortcut: Alt = across apps; Ctrl = across tabs.

practice.q: Which shortcut **closes the active program**?
practice.solution: **Alt+F4** closes the window in front. On the desktop, it opens the shutdown dialog.

practice.q: **Win + Left arrow** does what to the current window?
options: Snaps it to the left half of the screen
Moves it to another monitor only
practice.solution: **Snap**: Win+Left/Right parks the window on that half; Win+Up maximises; Win+Down restores or minimises.

practice.q: While holding **Alt**, pressing **Shift+Tab** in the switcher —
options: Moves through the windows in the reverse direction
practice.solution: Shift reverses direction in almost every Windows cycle — in Alt+Tab it walks the window list backwards.

practice.q: Which shortcut **pastes** copied content?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+V** pastes; Ctrl+X cuts, Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+P prints.

practice.q: **Ctrl+Y** in MS Word —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Y = redo** (it can also repeat the last action). Undo is Ctrl+Z.

practice.q: To **select the entire document** in one stroke, press —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+A** = select **A**ll — the whole document or every cells/rows in the active region.

practice.q: Which shortcut **inserts a hyperlink** in Word or Excel?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+K** opens the hyperlink dialog (K sits next to L for 'link' on the keyboard).

practice.q: Which shortcut makes selected text **bold**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+B** = bold, Ctrl+I = italic, Ctrl+U = underline — the initial letters.

practice.q: Which shortcut **centres** the selected paragraph in Word?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+E = cEntre.** Ctrl+C is copy; C was taken, so centre borrowed E.

practice.q: The correct set of Word alignment shortcuts is —
practice.solution: **LERJ**: Left, cEntre, Right, Justify.
practice.shortcut: LERJ — left to right across the line.

practice.q: **Shift+F3** in MS Word —
options: Changes the case of selected text (lower/UPPER/Capitalise)
practice.solution: **Shift+F3** cycles the case of the selection in Word — press repeatedly to march lower → UPPER → Capitalise Each Word. (In Excel, plain Shift+F3 opens Insert Function instead.)

practice.q: Which shortcut jumps to the **beginning of the document**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Home** = document start; **Ctrl+End** = document end.

practice.q: In Word, **Ctrl+G** opens the same dialog as —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+G and F5 both open Go To**, for jumping to a page, section or line number.

practice.q: Which shortcut closes the **current document** without closing the Word application?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+W** (or Ctrl+F4) closes the document window; **Alt+F4** quits the whole program.

practice.q: In **MS Word**, Ctrl+D opens the —
practice.solution: Ctrl+D opens the **Font** dialog in Word. 'Duplicate' belongs to PowerPoint (Ctrl+D duplicates a slide/object); fill-down is Excel's Ctrl+D.
practice.shortcut: Same key, three apps, three jobs.

practice.q: The **Office key that saves with a new name/ location** (Save As) is —
practice.solution: **F12 = Save As** in Word, Excel and PowerPoint. Plain save stays Ctrl+S.

practice.q: Which statement is **correct**?
practice.solution: The undo pair is **Ctrl+Z (undo) / Ctrl+Y (redo)**. The cut-copy pair is Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C; printing is Ctrl+P.
practice.shortcut: Z back, Y forward; X cuts, C copies.

practice.q:
Match the Word shortcut to its effect:
A. Ctrl+J  B. Ctrl+2  C. Shift+F3  D. Ctrl+U
options: A-underline, B-change case, C-double spacing, D-justify
A-justify, B-double spacing, C-change case, D-underline
A-justify, B-change case, C-double spacing, D-underline
A-double spacing, B-justify, C-underline, D-change case
practice.solution: Ctrl+**J** = **J**ustify; Ctrl+**2** = double spacing; Shift+**F3** = case cycling; Ctrl+**U** = **U**nderline.

practice.q: In MS Excel, **Ctrl+Home** moves the cell pointer to —
options: The top of the visible screen
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Home** = A1. Ctrl+End = the last used cell of the sheet.

practice.q: Which shortcut moves to the **next worksheet** in the same workbook?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+PgDn / Ctrl+PgUp** flip through the sheet tabs.
practice.shortcut: Page = the next sheet of the book.

practice.q: In Excel, **Ctrl+End** takes you to —
options: The bottom of the current column only
A new row at the very end
The last used cell of the worksheet
practice.solution: **Ctrl+End** jumps to the bottom-right of the used range — the last cell holding data or formatting.
practice.shortcut: End of what you actually used.

practice.q: Which shortcut selects the **entire row** containing the active cell?
practice.solution: **Shift+Space = row**, Ctrl+Space = column.

practice.q: To select the **entire worksheet** at once, press —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+A** selects all; one press covers the sheet (a second press extends it in older versions).

practice.q: Which key **edits the active cell** in Excel?
practice.solution: **F2** puts the cell in edit mode — the keyboard version of a double-click.

practice.q: While typing in a cell, which shortcut starts a **new line within the same cell**?
practice.solution: **Alt+Enter** inserts a line break inside the cell. Ctrl+Enter fills all selected cells with the entry instead.

practice.q: Which shortcut **copies the contents of the cell above** into the active cell?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+D = fill down** (from the cell above); **Ctrl+R = fill right**.

practice.q: Which shortcut inserts **today's date** into the active cell?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+;** stamps the date; **Ctrl+Shift+;** stamps the current time.

practice.q: Which statement about **F4** in Excel is correct?
options: It cycles a cell reference between absolute, mixed and relative forms
It opens the Format Cells dialog
practice.solution: **F4** toggles absolute/mixed/relative addressing while editing a reference (and repeats the last action outside edit mode). Format Cells is Ctrl+1; saving is Ctrl+S.

practice.q: The shortcut to start a **slide show from the beginning** is —
practice.solution: **F5** runs the show from slide 1; **Shift+F5** starts from the current slide.

practice.q: During a slideshow, pressing **B** turns the screen —
practice.solution: **B = black screen, W = white screen**; press the same key again to bring the slide back.

practice.q: Which shortcut ends a running **slideshow**?
practice.solution: **Esc** ends the show and returns to the editor.

practice.q: Which shortcut starts the slideshow **from the current slide**?
practice.solution: **Shift+F5** previews from the slide you are editing — ideal when polishing one slide.

practice.q: In PowerPoint, **Ctrl+M** —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+M** adds a new slide (M = 'more slides').

practice.q:
Match the Excel shortcut:
A. Ctrl+D  B. Ctrl+R  C. Ctrl+;  D. Alt+Enter
options: A-fill right, B-fill down, C-current time, D-new line in cell
A-fill down, B-fill right, C-current date, D-new line in cell
A-fill down, B-new line in cell, C-current date, D-fill right
A-current date, B-fill right, C-fill down, D-new line in cell
practice.solution: **D down, R right, ; date, Alt+Enter line-break.**

practice.q: Which shortcut opens a **new tab** in a web browser?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+T** = new tab; Ctrl+N = new whole window; Ctrl+Tab = move to the next existing tab.

practice.q: Which shortcut **closes the current browser tab**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+W** (or Ctrl+F4) closes the tab; Alt+F4 would close the entire browser window.

practice.q: Which shortcut **reopens the last closed tab**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+T** is the undo of Ctrl+W — it restores recently closed tabs one by one.

practice.q: In a browser, **Ctrl+9** jumps to —
practice.solution: Ctrl+1–8 pick tab numbers 1–8, but **Ctrl+9 always goes to the rightmost (last) tab**, however many are open.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens an **Incognito (private) window** in Chrome/Edge?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N** — Chrome and Edge. Firefox uses Ctrl+Shift+P.

practice.q: In **Mozilla Firefox**, a private browsing window opens with —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+P** = Private window in Firefox. (The same keys open the Print dialog in Chrome/Edge.)

practice.q: Which shortcut opens the **Clear browsing data** dialog?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+Delete** opens the panel to wipe history, cookies and cache.

practice.q: Which shortcut goes **back to the previous page** in a browser?
practice.solution: **Alt+Left = back, Alt+Right = forward** — history direction keys.

practice.q: **Ctrl+D** in a web browser —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+D = bookmark** ('D for done reading'). Downloads are Ctrl+J.

practice.q: Which shortcut toggles the **bookmarks bar**?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+B** shows or hides the bookmarks bar; plain Ctrl+B is bold in documents.

practice.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Ctrl+H shows history but Ctrl+H in Word opens Replace
Ctrl+H shows history in every program
Ctrl+D bookmarks a page and duplicates slides in Word
Alt+Home opens the browser's download page
practice.solution: Ctrl+H is **History in browsers, Replace in Word** — same keys, different apps. Ctrl+D duplicates slides in PowerPoint, not Word; the browser home page is Alt+Home (that part of option D is right but its download-page tail is wrong).
practice.shortcut: Same key, three apps, three jobs.

practice.q: In a web browser, **Ctrl+J** opens —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+J = Downloads** list — J for the 'just fetched' files.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens the **browser history** page?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+H = History** in Chrome, Edge and Firefox.

practice.q: Which shortcut switches the browser to **full screen**?
practice.solution: **F11** toggles full screen; F5 reloads; F12 opens developer tools.

practice.q:
Match the app to its private-window shortcut:
A. Chrome  B. Edge  C. Firefox
practice.solution: Chrome and Edge (Chromium family) share **Ctrl+Shift+N**; only Firefox uses **Ctrl+Shift+P**.

practice.q: Which function key opens **Help** in most programs?
practice.solution: **F1** is the universal help key — one key, one demand for help.

practice.q: Which function key **renames** a selected file or folder?
practice.solution: **F2** renames in File Explorer and edits the active cell in Excel — a second look at the item.

practice.q: Which function key **refreshes** the desktop or a web page?
practice.solution: **F5** refreshes; Ctrl+F5 reloads even harder (ignoring the cache).

practice.q: Which function key opens the **Save As** dialog in MS Word?
practice.solution: **F12 = Save As** in all Office apps; plain saving stays on Ctrl+S.

practice.q: Pressing **F3** in File Explorer opens —
practice.solution: **F3** opens the search box in File Explorer (in Word, Shift+F3 cycles letter case instead).

practice.q: Which function key runs the **Spelling & Grammar** check in MS Word?
practice.solution: **F7** spells — in Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

practice.q: In MS Excel, which key **edits the active cell**?
practice.solution: **F2** puts the cell into edit mode (rename in Explorer, edit in Excel).

practice.q: **Shift+F11** in MS Excel —
practice.solution: **Shift+F11** adds a fresh worksheet; plain **F11** turns the selection into a **chart sheet**.

practice.q: In MS Word, **F5** opens the —
practice.solution: In Word, F5 (like Ctrl+G) opens **Go To** for jumping to a page or line. The slideshow F5 belongs to PowerPoint.
practice.shortcut: F5 by app: Word = go, PPT = show.

practice.q: Which combination **closes the active program**?
practice.solution: **Alt+F4** quits the program; **Ctrl+F4** closes only the current document or tab inside it.

practice.q: **Shift+F10** —
practice.solution: **Shift+F10** = the keyboard's right-click; F10 alone highlights the menu bar.

practice.q: Which combination closes **only the current document**, keeping the application open?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+F4** closes the document window inside the app; **Alt+F4** closes the app itself.
practice.shortcut: Ctrl = close content; Alt = close app.

practice.q: Which pair is **correctly matched**?
options: F10 — activates the menu bar; Shift+F10 — right-click menu
practice.solution: **F10** lights up the menu bar; add **Shift** and it behaves as the right-click at your cursor. Refresh is F5, spellcheck F7, help F1, rename F2.

practice.q: In a web browser, **F12** opens —
practice.solution: F12 flips meaning by app: **Save As in Office, developer tools in browsers**.
practice.shortcut: F12 in a browser = build mode.

practice.q: In MS Excel, **F11** creates —
options: A chart sheet from the selected data
practice.solution: **F11** = chart on its own sheet; **Shift+F11** = new blank worksheet; F11 in a **browser** = full screen.

practice.q: Traditionally, pressing which key **during Windows start-up** entered Safe Mode?
practice.solution: **F8** at boot opened the advanced start-up menu with Safe Mode on older Windows versions — a classic exam fact.

practice.q: Which statement about **F5** is correct?
options: It refreshes a web page and starts the slideshow in PowerPoint
It saves the file in Word
practice.solution: F5 = **refresh/reload** on desktops and browsers, **slideshow** in PowerPoint, **Go To** in Word. Spellcheck is F7; save-as is F12; closing is Alt+F4.

practice.q:
Arrange the function-key ladder correctly:
Help, Rename, Refresh, Save As (Office)
practice.solution: Help = **F1**, rename = **F2**, refresh = **F5**, Save As = **F12**.
